name: Indonesian
confidence_why: Whether Indonesian has word stress at all is an open debate: Cohn & McCarthy 1994, Halim 1981 and Soderberg & Olson 2008 describe fixed penultimate stress (final after a schwa penult), while the instrumental and perception experiments of van Zanten & van Heuven 1998, Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 and van Zanten & Goedemans 2009 find no word stress in the dominant Javanese-influenced variety, only a phrasal accent on one of the last two syllables, and Farinella, Kaland & Kaufman 2025 find word-level penultimate prominence in eastern speakers but not in a Javanese speaker, so the answer depends on the speaker's substrate and the status of the standard variety is still contested.
catalog_citation: Goedemans, Rob & Ellen van Zanten. 2007. Stress and accent in Indonesian. In V.J. van Heuven & E. van Zanten (eds), Prosody in Indonesian languages (LOT Occasional Series 9), 35-62. Utrecht: LOT.
catalog_locator: sec. 3.5.1 'The status of word stress in Indonesian', p. 54 and p. 56; sec. 3.6 'Conclusion', p. 59
catalog_quote: It appears, however, that accent location in Indonesian as spoken by Javanese speakers is not associated to any particular syllable. Consequently, we must conclude that this variant has no need for word stress. There are no phonetic correlates for it, neither is it used at the abstract phonological level. We claim, then, that the Javanese variant does not have word stress, and will, from now on, consider prominence in this variant to be the result of accent only. ... However, even if we would take the term Indonesian to cover its most common variant (Javanese Indonesian), the claim that stress is penultimate cannot be maintained. On the contrary, we have found compelling evidence for the claim that this variant does not have stress at all. ... In our view, the rule that drives prominence patterns in the influential Javanese variety of Indonesian is phrasal. Possibly, the only phonological rule that is relevant for accent location in Indonesian states that it must occur somewhere at the right edge of the phrase. Since there is no evidence for strict patterning of the main stress, we think any proposal that describes the patterning of secondary stresses with respect to the main stress must be received with great caution.
sweep_summary: indo1316 (Standard Indonesian) is in the catalog with deciding quote from Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 (pp.36, 56, held in full): no word stress, accent domain = phrase (the catalog_kind 'fixed-dominant' vs that quote is already flagged in the stin1234 check record). Three works with stress in the title, all about word stress in this language. (1) van Zanten, Goedemans & Pacilly 2003 (Benjamins, paywalled; Crossref/jbe-platform show no OA copy; Leiden repository and every search engine could not be reached by automated download): Google Books snippets of its conclusion — 'good reason to exclude the penultimate stress hypothesis.. the rule that drives prominence patterns in the influential Javanese variety of Indonesian is phrasal.. prominence may freely occur on any of the last two syllables (and sometimes even the antepenult) of any word.. [Javanese variant] may have a phrasal accent only' — CONFIRM the catalog's classification; it is the earlier (Jakartan-listener) report of the experiments written up in the held 2007 chapter (G&vZ 2007 fn.4 p.48), so it does not supersede the deciding source. (2) Odé & van Heuven (eds) 1994, Semaian 9 (HathiTrust search-only at Michigan, Google Books snippet view; no open copy): Laksman's chapter (pp.108-139) reports experimental penultimate stress in disyllabic words — p.133 'Stress was invariably perceived on the penultimate syllable. Therefore, I conclude that one of these two parameters (Fo and duration) characterizes the stress' — and that schwa can be stressed; on its own terms it CONTRADICTS the no-word-stress coding, but the same Leiden group later called that view 'no longer defensible' (van Heuven & van Zanten 2007: 194, held) and cites it only for 'schwa can be stressed'/'a tendency, not an absolute rule'. Medium priority to acquire the Laksman chapter (print: U Michigan, MPI-EVA). (3) Samsuri 1971 (Nusa Indah, Ende; paper from the 1968 Seminar Bahasa Indonesia; Google Books snippet view of the original-spelling booklet 3tlBAQAAIAAJ and the proceedings I4hbAAAAIAAJ): three degrees of stress (lemah/biasa/keras), stress non-phonemic ('tidak fonemis'; changing its position changes no meaning), and strong stress on the final syllable of words/phrases in isolation ('suku achir mendapat tekanan jang keras') — the 'final stress hypothesis' of the literature (G&vZ 2007: 39; vZ&G 2009: 198; Roosman 2007: 91); CONTRADICTS the catalog's classification but is impressionistic and superseded; low priority. Best new statement = the 2003 conclusion (snippet-only), confirming, not superseding, the held 2007 deciding source.bib, Crossref, HathiTrust bib API, OpenLibrary, 60+ Google Books GData snippet files) and copies of the held 2007/2009 Leiden texts are under with. the legacy Google Books GData feed and Glottolog.bib endpoints were the working channels.

new_statements.quote: In Indonesian, word stress has traditionally been described as being fixed on the penultimate syllable. If this rule holds good, stress should help listeners identify words. The results of the present experiment indicate that this is not the case, however. [p. 141] ... Word stress information was not used by our Indonesian listeners to differentiate between words. Our results indicate that stress is communicatively irrelevant and essentially free in Indonesian. They support the view advanced by Halim (1974:111-3) and Zubkova (1966, cited in Odé 1994) that there is no word stress in Indonesian, free stress being tantamount to no stress. [p. 142]

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog record (StressTyp2: penultimate stress, stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable)): the paper explicitly tests and rejects the fixed-penultimate description and concludes there is no word stress. It agrees with the existing_statement from van Zanten, Goedemans & Pacilly 2003 (no word-level stress; prominence is phrasal) and with the catalog's deciding 2007 source as summarized there. Speaker: one Balinese-Indonesian news reader; listeners: two of Balinese, three of Sundanese and one of Javanese descent, resident in the Netherlands (p. 135).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A gating/identification experiment: segmentally identical, prosodically different stimuli (e.g. ada / adalah / adakala truncated) were not identified above chance by five of six Indonesian listeners, while Dutch listeners did better. The authors conclude that stress position plays no role in word identification, that stress is 'communicatively irrelevant and essentially free', and that this supports Halim (1974) and Zubkova (1966): Indonesian has no word stress. They report the traditional description (penultimate stress; Dardjowidjojo 1978, Teeuw 1978, Cohn 1989) only as the hypothesis being tested, and note that phonetically stress is only weakly marked. (The text reads 'citecl'in' for 'cited in'; corrected in the quote.)
new_statements.exceptions: p. 142: an earlier study (van Zanten & van Heuven, submitted) found a preference for stress on phonologically heavy prefinal syllables, but sets with heavy prefinal syllables were not identified any better, so 'such a preference has no relevance in speech communication'. p. 130 (citing others): Laksman 1994 found schwa can be stressed; Halim 1974 places the sentence-based accent on the final syllable before an internal boundary and on the penult of the sentence-final word.
new_statements.identity_note: Mayer 1906 describes Netherlands-Indies 'Maleisch' (colonial Malay, c. 1895-1906, Dutch orthography), the precursor of standard Indonesian rather than modern Bahasa Indonesia. Van Zanten & van Heuven 1998 used one Balinese-Indonesian speaker and six Indonesian listeners of Balinese, Sundanese and Javanese descent living in the Netherlands, i.e. Indonesian as spoken by substrate-language speakers; the existing 2003 statement concerns the Javanese-substrate variety specifically. Musgrave 2001 treats standard written Indonesian (syntax only).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is very weak and falls on the penultimate syllable; if the penult has the 'mute' vowel (schwa, written ĕ), stress falls on the final syllable instead; the rule holds for suffixed words too (i.e. it applies to the penult of the whole suffixed word). The same page notes that ĕ is mostly heard in the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Penult containing schwa: stress goes to the final syllable. 'Gewoonlijk' (usually) leaves room for unstated exceptions; stress described as very weak.

readall_conflicts: The two opened sources with a stress statement disagree, and the disagreement is the same one already inside the catalog. Mayer 1906 (p. VIII) gives the traditional rule: very weak stress on the penult, shifting to the final syllable when the penult vowel is schwa, suffixed words included; this matches the catalog's StressTyp2 record (penultimate). Van Zanten & van Heuven 1998 (pp. 141-142) test exactly that traditional penultimate rule with an identification experiment and reject it: Indonesian listeners do not use stress to identify words, stress is 'communicatively irrelevant and essentially free', and the authors endorse Halim (1974) and Zubkova (1966) that there is no word stress; this matches the existing 2003 statement and the catalog's deciding 2007 chapter. The 1998 paper also reports (p. 130) that Halim's sentence-based accent falls on the penult of the sentence-final word, which explains why impressionistic descriptions such as Mayer's hear penultimate stress. Musgrave 2001 is silent; the 2014 chapter could not be opened. The standing tension inside the catalog remains as before: the StressTyp2 record's pattern string (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) encodes penultimate main stress with alternating secondaries, whereas the catalog's deciding source (Goedemans & van Zanten 2007, echoed by van Zanten, Goedemans & Pacilly 2003 in existing_statements) holds that Javanese-substrate Indonesian has no word-level stre…

Fallback if the catalog keeps a 'penult reading' row in the dominant set: primary-only penult, no secondary rhythm — penultimate stress — per Halim 1981:56,58, Lapoliwa 1981:31,128 ('only one degree of stress'), Soderberg & Olson 2008:211, Macdonald & Soenjono 1967:31; the coded initial+alternating secondaries (1010, 101010, 1001010..) rest on Cohn 1989's impressionistic data alone (Cohn & McCarthy 1994 fn.3). sources.quote: 'Early, impressionistic studies claimed that stress regularly occurs on the penultimate syllable, but shifts to the final syllable when the penult contains schwa (Cohn, 1989; Halim, 1981; Stoel, 2007)... However, recent work rejects the claim that Indonesian displays any evidence of regular word-level stress, claiming instead that the language is stressless (Athanasopoulou et al., 2021; Goedemans & van Zanten, 2014; Odé & van Heuven, 1994).' Own finding: gesture aligns to word-penult in eastern varieties (word-based) and to final syllables, phrase-based, in the Javanese variety.

sources.note: Perception study framed on Indonesian being a non-tonal (intonation) language: one-word utterances can carry four intonation contours (H emphatic, LH interrogative, L doubting, HL neutral) with pragmatic, not lexical, meanings; pitch distinctions in Indonesian operate post-lexically; contact with Mandarin 'has not resulted in the adoption of lexical tone in the Indonesian language'. tone.quote: What is interesting is that a word in Indonesian may represent a clause or an elliptical clause that only contains one utterance and it may carry with itself tonal properties which resemble the feature of lexical tones yet maintain its function as an intonational expression with distinct meanings (dependent on the preceding sentence or context in which they occur). Historically, the Mandarin tonal system has incorporated its way into Indonesian through contact between the two languages. However, such language context has not resulted in the adoption of lexical tone in the Indonesian language.

tone.quote: Stress in Indonesian is predictable. Unaffixed words in isolation have primary stress on the penultimate syllable, but if the vowel in the penultimate syllable is a schwa /ə/, the stress usually occurs on the ultimate syllable (depending on the dialect).

tone.quote: The word accent in IN is non-distinctive in the sense that it is never used to differentiate lexical meaning. The word accent of IN may be termed 'tonotemporal', in the sense that it is a kind of prominence characterised by the pitch of the voice - thus, tonal -, and by the length of time (duration) in which the accentuated syllable is pronounced - thus, temporal -, rather than by intensity. [...] It was shown that three pitch levels needed to be recognised [...] These pitch levels are relative rather than absolute. [...] There is no word-accent as such in IN. That is, neither the strength nor the placement of accent within a word carries any lexical difference.

sources.quote: [p.133, Laksman] "Stress was invariably perceived on the penultimate syllable. Therefore, I conclude that one of these two parameters (Fo and duration) characterizes the stress. The stress marking of words in a carrier-sentence is more or less reflected in final words of NPs positioned after the verb." [p.38, Odé's survey] "... the central vowel [ə] is always unaccented, we have found that it can be accented as well as all other vowels." In her conclusion Laksman states that, generally speaking, [in disyllabic words accent is realized in the penultimate ...] stress is still perceived in the penultimate syllable." [pp.38-40] "1. In isolation: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by pitch obtrusion in that syllable, even if the vowel is a pepet. 2. Before a verb: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by duration, even if there is pitch obtrusion in the final syllable or if the word is not (pitch-)accented. 3. After a verb: word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized by pitch obtrusion 'en finale de la phrase' (Laksman [n.d.]: 78)"
